content: Accumulating evidence indicates that prenatal exposure to antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) is associated with an increased risk of physical anomalies and neurodevelopmental impairments in children. Neurodevelopmental impairments can manifest as specific deficits or a combination of deficits in cognitive, motor, and social skills, which may be transient or persist into adulthood. It is critical to identify, minimize, and clearly communicate these risks to women with epilepsy. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of prenatal exposure to commonly prescribed AEDs on the neurodevelopmental outcomes of children. Additionally, the methodological quality of the evidence was assessed. The study included prospective cohort studies, pregnancy registry-based cohort studies, and randomized controlled trials. Participants were women with epilepsy who were either taking AEDs or not taking AEDs during pregnancy, as well as women without epilepsy as a control group. The analysis included 22 prospective cohort studies and six registry-based studies. The quality of the studies varied, with more recent studies demonstrating improved methodological rigor, such as larger sample sizes and blinded assessments of individual AED outcomes. Children exposed to carbamazepine (CBZ) during pregnancy had a lower developmental quotient (DQ) compared to children born to women without epilepsy (mean difference [MD] -5.58, 95% confidence interval [CI] -10.83 to -0.34, P = 0.04). Similarly, children exposed to CBZ had a lower DQ compared to children of women with untreated epilepsy (MD -7.22, 95% CI -12.76 to -1.67, P = 0.01). However, further analysis using a random-effects model suggested that these findings were influenced by variability within the studies, and no significant association with CBZ was observed. The intelligence quotient (IQ) of older children exposed to CBZ was not significantly different from that of children born to women without epilepsy or those with untreated epilepsy. In contrast, children exposed to sodium valproate (VPA) had significantly lower DQ and IQ scores compared to children of women with untreated epilepsy and those without epilepsy. For example, the IQ of children exposed to VPA was lower than that of children born to women without epilepsy (MD -8.94, 95% CI -11.96 to -5.92, P < 0.00001) and lower than children of women with untreated epilepsy (MD -8.17, 95% CI -12.80 to -3.55, P = 0.0005). A dose-dependent effect was observed for VPA, with higher doses (800 to 1000 mg daily or above) associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in children. When comparing AEDs, the IQ of children exposed to VPA was significantly lower than that of children exposed to CBZ (MD 8.69, 95% CI 5.51 to 11.87, P < 0.00001). Similarly, children exposed to VPA had lower IQ scores compared to those exposed to lamotrigine (LTG) (MD -10.80, 95% CI -14.42 to -7.17, P < 0.00001) and phenytoin (PHT) (MD 9.25, 95% CI 4.78 to 13.72, P < 0.0001). In contrast, no significant differences in IQ or DQ were observed between children exposed to CBZ and those exposed to LTG or PHT. The findings highlight that prenatal exposure to VPA is associated with a significant reduction in IQ, which may have long-term implications for educational and occupational outcomes. However, for some women, VPA remains the most effective medication for controlling seizures. Therefore, treatment decisions should involve detailed counseling about these risks, both at the initiation of treatment and during pre-conception counseling. While most women with epilepsy should continue their medication during pregnancy to avoid the risks associated with uncontrolled seizures, further research is needed to evaluate the effects of newer AEDs, which are increasingly prescribed.
